answer.exemplar: A principal component is the unit direction, taken through the mean of the centred data, along which the variance of the projected data is largest among all directions. A model answer should set up the variance of the projection as the quadratic form in the direction, that is the scalar whose vector transpose times the covariance matrix times the vector, and then say that maximising it subject to a unit direction is a constrained optimisation whose critical points satisfy the eigenvector equation, so the maximising directions are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix and the maximum value is the largest eigenvalue. It should add that the data are centred first so the projection measures spread rather than location, and that the retained share of the total variance is that eigenvalue over the trace, since the trace is the sum of the eigenvalues.

questions.explanation: Tying the eigenvalue to the variance is the step most often skipped, and without it the construction looks like an arbitrary algebraic choice rather than an optimisation. The constraint that the direction has unit length is what forces a multiplier and produces the eigenvector equation, so a model answer has to show the quadratic form and the constraint together. Saying that the total variance is the trace is what turns a single eigenvalue into a proportion of the whole.
questions.hint: Write the variance of the projection as a quadratic form, then maximise it subject to unit length.

questions.explanation: A diagonalisation collects independent eigenvectors into a basis, so exactly as many independent eigenvectors as the order of the matrix are needed, and the independence rather than the distinctness is the requirement. Distinct eigenvalues are sufficient but not necessary, since a matrix with a repeated eigenvalue can still be diagonalised when the eigenspace for that value is large enough, which is what the matrix twice the identity demonstrates. Symmetry is far stronger than needed, and a zero eigenvalue obstructs nothing, since a diagonal matrix may have a zero on its diagonal.

answer.exemplar: A symmetric matrix is positive definite when the quadratic form it builds, the scalar whose vector transpose times the matrix times the vector, is strictly positive for every nonzero vector, and zero for the zero vector. A model answer should connect this to eigenvalues, since a symmetric matrix has an orthonormal eigenbasis and the quadratic form evaluated on a unit eigenvector equals the eigenvalue, so positivity of the form is the same statement as every eigenvalue being positive. It should add the consequences: the matrix is invertible, the minimum of the form over the unit sphere is the smallest eigenvalue, and the leading principal minors are all positive by Sylvester's criterion, which gives a way to test the property without computing eigenvalues at all.

questions.explanation: The eigenvalue route is the one that connects the definition to everything else, since the extremal behaviour of the form on the unit sphere is exactly the smallest and largest eigenvalues. A model answer that only restates the definition, or that asserts invertibility without the eigenvalue argument, leaves the consequences unmotivated. Mentioning Sylvester's criterion earns credit because it shows the property is testable from the entries alone.
questions.hint: Evaluate the form on a unit eigenvector to read off an eigenvalue, then reason from the sign.

answer.exemplar: The change-of-basis matrix has the new basis vectors as its columns, and expressing a vector in the new basis means solving a system whose coefficient matrix is that matrix, so a solution is guaranteed for every vector only when the matrix is invertible. A model answer should add that invertibility of the new basis follows from its independence, since a dependent set of basis vectors could not be a basis at all, and that the inverse is what takes coordinates back. It should then say what fails without it: a zero determinant, a lost solution, a collapse of the space onto a proper subspace, and the absence of any way to recover the original coordinates, so the transformation is one-way and information is destroyed.

questions.explanation: The point is not that the matrix ought to be invertible by convention but that invertibility is what guarantees a solution for every vector, so the argument has to be made through solving a system. Tying it back to independence of the basis vectors closes the loop, since that is where invertibility comes from. Saying only that an inverse is needed to go back is too weak, because it does not explain why one exists.
questions.hint: Think of coordinate conversion as solving a linear system with the new basis vectors as columns.
